extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, early-career researchers, and learners of mathematics (math enthusiasts and practicing mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of practical guidelines and philosophical principles for learning mathematics, solving problems, conducting research, and managing a mathematical career, distilled from Terence Tao's quotes and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; learn outside it
rubrics_metrics.description: "Learn and relearn your field, but don't be afraid to learn things outside your field."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously revisit and update foundational knowledge while also studying adjacent or distant fields to create new connections and insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dig deeper than statement-and-proof
rubrics_metrics.description: "Just because you know a statement and proof of Fundamental Lemma X, you shouldn't take that lemma for granted; instead, you should dig deeper until you really understand what the lemma is all about."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True understanding requires probing hypotheses, exploring alternative proofs, examining intuition and context, not mere memorization of statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain to others to test understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you can't explain the solution of a problem to a classmate, then you haven't really understood the solution yourself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being able to teach or clearly explain a solution reveals gaps; use exposition and peer explanation as a diagnostic for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask simple ('dumb') questions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ask yourself dumb questions – and answer them!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge basic assumptions with simple questions; these often expose foundational structure and lead to deep insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active engagement over passive learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mathematics is not a spectator sport. You have to actively engage with the concepts to truly understand them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize problem solving, doing examples, and active manipulation of concepts rather than only listening or reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write or lecture for deeper learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is particularly useful to lecture on your field, or write lecture notes or other expository material, even if it is just for your own personal use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizing material for others forces clarity and consolidates your knowledge; creating expository notes is a productive learning tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks outside your field even if partial
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't expect to understand 100% of any given talk, especially if it is in a field you are not familiar with; as long as you learn something, the effort is not wasted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to unfamiliar talks yields incremental learning and serendipitous ideas; partial comprehension is still valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accessible resources pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: "The accuracy of Wikipedia can be dodgy in some places, but in maths, it's really quite good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ modern, easily accessible references (e.g., Wikipedia) as starting points while remaining critical and verifying with authoritative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress by next attainable step (ledge analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "You want to get to the top of the cliff. But that's not what you focus on immediately. You focus on the next ledge just beyond your reach."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose large problems into immediate, achievable steps; incremental progress is the practical path to hard goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try techniques even if they won't fully solve
rubrics_metrics.description: "It can often be profitable to try a technique on a problem even if you know in advance that it cannot possibly solve the problem completely."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting imperfect methods can yield partial results, new perspectives, or useful lemmas that advance understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the problem-solving journey
rubrics_metrics.description: "The journey of solving a problem is often more rewarding than the solution itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize process, learning, and satisfaction from exploration rather than fixation on final answers alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics emphasizes process over answers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The act of solving problems is what mathematics is all about. Mathematics is not about answers, it is about the process of finding the answers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on methods, heuristics, and reasoning strategies as central mathematical achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: "In your research, be both flexible and patient."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt methods when needed and accept long timelines; persistence and adaptability are research virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work; discard when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Be sceptical of your own work, and don't be afraid to use the wastebasket."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply critical self-review and be willing to abandon unproductive approaches or write-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target boundary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "What's really interesting are the problems just at the boundary between what we can do relatively easily and what are hopeless."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek problems that stretch existing techniques—these often yield the most fertile ground for progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract away inessential components
rubrics_metrics.description: "By moving the inessential components of a problem, you can focus on what's really going on."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify problems by removing peripheral details to expose core structure and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent vs development: nurture matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Talent is important, but how one develops and nurtures it is even more so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize deliberate practice, habits, mentorship, and environment over reliance on innate ability alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius not required to do mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Does one have to be a genius to do mathematics? The answer is an emphatic NO."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical success is accessible through sustained effort, not reserved for a mythical genius class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard work over romanticised eureka moments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mathematical breakthroughs are not powered solely (or even primarily) by 'Eureka' moments of genius, but are in fact largely a product of hard work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect steady, methodical effort and incremental advances rather than sudden inspiration as the engine of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on last-minute intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Relying on intelligence alone to pull things off at the last minute may work for a while, but, generally speaking, at the graduate level or higher it doesn't."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop sustained study habits and deep preparation rather than ad-hoc cramming or shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with problems; be methodical
rubrics_metrics.description: "I don't have any magical ability. I look at a problem, play with it, work out a strategy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine experimentation and playful exploration with deliberate strategic planning in problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess ease can hinder long-term growth
rubrics_metrics.description: "In some cases, an abundance of raw talent may end up (somewhat perversely) to actually be harmful for one's long-term mathematical development."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encountering difficulty builds skills and resilience; avoid situations that prevent development by making everything trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't choose career based on glamour
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't base career decisions on glamour or fame."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select problems, positions, and directions based on genuine interest and sustainability rather than prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoyment sustains sustained effort
rubrics_metrics.description: "To really get anywhere in mathematics requires hard work. If you don't enjoy what you are doing... it will be difficult to put in the sustained amounts of energy required to succeed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intrinsic motivation and choose work you find enjoyable to maintain long-term productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration broadens understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "Collaboration is very important for me, as it allows me to learn about other fields, and, conversely, to share what I have learned about my own fields with others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with others to gain new perspectives, learn techniques, and disseminate ideas; collaboration is a central research tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't obsess prematurely on 'big problems'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't prematurely obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a broad base and explore varied problems before committing to a single grand focus too early in a career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down and share work early
rubrics_metrics.description: "Write down what you've done, and make your work available."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document progress and circulate drafts or notes to solicit feedback and contribute to the community even at preliminary stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to increase understanding, not rank
rubrics_metrics.description: "The objective in mathematics is not to obtain the highest ranking... instead, it is to increase understanding of mathematics (both for yourself, and for your colleagues and students)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize intellectual contribution and clarity of understanding over competition or status metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work across fields; see mathematics as unified
rubrics_metrics.description: "I tend to view mathematics as a unified subject and am particularly happy when I get the opportunity to work on a project that involves several fields at once."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek interdisciplinary projects within mathematics to exploit connections and create novel methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relentless desire for complete understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "If I don't understand something properly, every single component, it really bugs me."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate curiosity and intolerance for shallow understanding; pursue clarity down to fundamental components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics allows rule-creation and exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: "The beauty of mathematics lies in that you can change the rules as you like, which is something that cannot be done in any other field."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the freedom of mathematical abstraction to explore alternative frameworks and construct new, internally consistent worlds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept advice that resonates with you
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ultimately you should follow advice not because someone tells you to, but because it was something that you already knew you should be doing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internalize and apply guidance that aligns with your own judgement; avoid dogmatic following of advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a life beyond work
rubrics_metrics.description: "My life is more than just my work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve work-life balance and recognize non-work aspects of life as important for long-term wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness fosters mathematical interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think the most important thing for developing an interest in mathematics is to have the ability and the freedom to play with mathematics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage experimental, low-stakes exploration to build curiosity and sustained interest in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giftedness doesn't remove educational complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Education is a complex, multifaceted, and painstaking process, and being gifted does not make this less so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide thoughtful, nuanced support and instruction even for gifted learners; progress still requires effort and scaffolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remain humble about honors
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is very humbling to receive the Fields Medal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat awards as recognition without letting them alter the fundamental work or motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abstraction (infinity) to simplify issues
rubrics_metrics.description: "Infinity absorbs a lot of sins."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ limits and infinite abstractions where appropriate to simplify arguments and avoid finite complications, while being mindful of rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as interplay: world, observations, models
rubrics_metrics.description: "Science is usually an interaction among three things: the real world, our observations of the real world, and the models of how we think the world works."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about how models relate to observations and reality; use modeling judiciously and check against empirical or logical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge personal subject-matter preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: "I was never very good at school with... humanities... anything which was more a matter of opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand personal strengths and weaknesses; tailor learning strategies to suit objective vs subjective areas as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek flow through deep concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you're concentrating hard, hours can fly by, and it's just you and a math problem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate conditions (focus, time blocks) that enable deep work and immersive problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core strategies: abstraction, decomposition, analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a certain way in which mathematicians approach problems. We abstract them. We break them up into pieces. We make analogies. We try to find connections with other problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these fundamental heuristics consistently: abstract essential structure, decompose into parts, seek analogies, and look for cross-problem connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiently eliminate wrong answers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The key to mathematics lies not only in finding an effective technical path but also in eliminating wrong answers among dozens of potentially applicable methods."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop heuristics and experience to quickly recognize and discard unpromising approaches to focus effort on promising directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas require detailed execution by originator
rubrics_metrics.description: "It would be very pleasant if one could just dream up the grand ideas and let some 'lesser mortals' fill in the details, but, trust me, it doesn't work like that at all in mathematics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to carry ideas through to detailed implementation and proofs; high-level ideas alone are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotate projects when stuck; document progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "I tend to have several things to work on at any given time; when I get stuck on one of them... I write up how far I managed to get, and turn attention to something else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain multiple projects, record partial progress, and switch focus to stay productive while ideas incubate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix gaps in skills as they irritate you
rubrics_metrics.description: "If there is something that I should know how to do but don't, it bugs me. I feel like I have to sit down and work out exactly what the problem is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to felt deficiencies by targeted learning until the gap is resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to identify dead-end techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: "It's not just about finding you know taking a technique that is going to work and applying it but you you need to not take the techniques that don't work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate experience to recognize, early, methods unlikely to succeed and avoid wasting effort on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about real-world impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most of what I do does not save lives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain perspective about the immediate practical impact of pure mathematical work and appreciate its intrinsic intellectual value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical research is self-directed
rubrics_metrics.description: "I remember having this vague idea that what mathematicians did was that some authority, someone, gave them problems to solve, and they just sort of solved them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that much mathematical research is driven by individual curiosity, problem-generation, and self-direction rather than externally assigned problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find motivation in understanding and explaining
rubrics_metrics.description: "For me, I guess the main motivation is the satisfaction of finally understanding some tricky mathematical concept or phenomenon and then explaining it to others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the joy of comprehension and the desire to communicate drive research and teaching efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards don't solve research problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "A shiny medal is not going to solve any of the problems I'm currently working on."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat honors as recognition but continue focusing on the substantive technical work that advances understanding.
